DOCUMENT:
Pricing Proposal: Weekend Rate Restructure
Harbourside Hotel, Revenue Management, April 2026

1. Proposal
From 1 June 2026 we propose to (a) raise the Best Available Rate (BAR) for Friday and Saturday nights from £145 to £165, and (b) introduce a two-night minimum for any stay that includes a Saturday night. Midweek rates are unchanged.

2. Context
Harbourside is a 112-room four-star hotel on the quay, with a leisure-led weekend business and a corporate-led midweek business. Our weekend BAR is £20 to £35 below the three comparable hotels in our competitive set, whose weekend rates currently range from £165 to £180. Weekend occupancy has recovered strongly since 2023 and we believe we are leaving money on the table.

Table 1. Weekend (Friday and Saturday) occupancy by month, 2025
Jan 62% | Feb 66% | Mar 74% | Apr 80% | May 85% | Jun 81%
Jul 89% | Aug 93% | Sep 88% | Oct 82% | Nov 72% | Dec 78%

Average weekend occupancy across 2025 was 79%. July and August are our strongest months, driven by the harbour festival and the school summer holidays, with September also benefiting from late-season visitors.

3. Evidence on price sensitivity
In the last week of June 2025 we raised the weekend BAR by £10, from £135 to the current £145. Weekend occupancy in July rose to 89%, from 81% in June. This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels; if anything, the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning as a quality option, and we expect the further increase to be absorbed in the same way.

This is consistent with feedback from our guest satisfaction surveys, where weekend guests rate "value for money" at 8.4 out of 10, the highest score among our competitive set.

4. Two-night minimum
Saturday nights are our most constrained inventory: we sold out on 31 Saturdays in 2025. Many of these guests stay only one night, leaving rooms empty on Friday or Sunday either side. A two-night minimum for stays including a Saturday will convert single-night Saturday stays into two-night stays and smooth occupancy across the weekend.

Our booking data show that weddings at Quayside Hall, the venue next door, account for around 38% of our Saturday-night room bookings. Wedding guests typically book as a block through the couple, arrive on the Saturday afternoon and check out on the Sunday morning.

5. Revenue impact
Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%, a £20 increase in BAR is worth about £204,000 a year in additional room revenue, before any gain from longer stays. We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above.

The two-night minimum should add further revenue through additional Friday and Sunday nights. We have not quantified this but expect it to be material, particularly in shoulder months.

6. Implementation and monitoring
The new rates will be loaded into the channel manager on 15 May for stays from 1 June, giving online travel agencies two weeks' notice. Corporate contracted rates and group rates already contracted will be honoured. We will review pick-up weekly against the same weeks in 2025 and report to the General Manager monthly. If weekend occupancy for any month falls more than five points below 2025, we will review the rate.

7. Recommendation
The evidence shows that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current rates and that we are priced well below our competitive set. We recommend approval of the £165 weekend BAR and the two-night Saturday minimum from 1 June 2026, delivering at least £204,000 of additional annual room revenue.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Across our 124 rooms, 104 weekend nights a year and average weekend occupancy of 79%" -- The hotel is described as a 112-room hotel in the Context section, but the revenue estimate uses 124 rooms. With 112 rooms the same calculation gives 112 x 104 x 0.79 x £20 = about £184,000, not £204,000.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "This tells us that our weekend guests are not price sensitive at current levels" -- The only evidence is that occupancy rose from June to July after a June rate rise, but the document itself says July and August are the strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. The seasonal rise confounds the comparison; it cannot show demand is price-insensitive (let alone that the higher price helped).
3. [missing_consideration] at: "We have assumed weekend occupancy is maintained at 2025 levels, which we consider prudent given the evidence above." -- The document states that about 38% of Saturday-night bookings are wedding guests from the adjacent venue who stay only Saturday night. A two-night minimum would exclude or deter this group, but the revenue case assumes occupancy is maintained and never addresses the loss of these single-night Saturday bookings.

REVIEW:
# Review: Weekend Rate Restructure Proposal

The case for a rate rise may well be sound, since you are priced £20–35 below a comparable set. But the three things you rely on for confidence (the June→July test, the "conservative" £204,000, and the low risk of the two-night minimum) don't hold up as written. A sceptical GM or finance director would likely spot each one.

## 1. The June→July "price test" doesn't show low price sensitivity

This is the proposal's central evidence, and it is confounded.

- **Seasonality explains the rise.** Your own Table 1 and text say July and August are your strongest months because of the harbour festival and school holidays. Occupancy rose from June to July, then rose again in August (93%) with no further price change. A June→July increase is what you would expect at any price.
- **Booking lead times.** The rise took effect in the last week of June. A good share of July weekend bookings, especially festival weekends, were probably made before then at £135. So July occupancy only partly reflects the new price.
- **One observation, no control.** Better tests would be:
  - July 2025 vs July 2024 (same season, different price)
  - Pick-up pace for July bookings made after the change vs before
  - Your weekend occupancy vs the comp set's over the same period

The conclusion ("not price sensitive… the higher rate appears to have reinforced our positioning") goes well beyond what one confounded month can support. I'd remove the causal claim or replace it with a proper comparison.

**Value for money (8.4).** This was measured at £145, the cheapest rate in the set. A high score is partly a consequence of being cheapest, so it doesn't predict how guests will respond at £165, where you would match the lowest competitor. It does suggest headroom exists, but it isn't evidence that the rise will be absorbed.

## 2. The £204,000 figure uses the wrong room count and isn't a floor

**Room count.** Section 2 says Harbourside has **112 rooms**. Section 5 calculates on **124**.

- 124 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£203,800** (the figure quoted)
- 112 × 104 × 79% × £20 ≈ **£184,000**

On the stated room count, the headline is overstated by about £20,000 before any other adjustment.

**Not every weekend room is sold at BAR.** The £20 uplift only applies to BAR-priced business. The proposal says corporate and contracted group rates will be honoured, and wedding blocks are 38% of Saturday bookings. You also need to deduct:

- Contracted group/wedding rooms
- Corporate, package and promotional rates
- OTA commission (typically 15–20% of the uplift on those channels)

Together these could plausibly cut the figure by a third or more. The calculation should apply the uplift only to the BAR-paying share of weekend room nights, net of commission.

**"Conservative" points the wrong way.** Assuming occupancy is unchanged leaves out the downside, which is the actual risk. Saying it "assumes no occupancy gain" makes the case sound conservative, but nobody expects a price rise to raise occupancy. The prudent framing is a range.

- **Break-even point:** £145 → £165 is a 13.8% rise. Revenue breaks even if weekend occupancy falls to about 69% (79% × 145/165), a drop of roughly 9–10 points.
- **Suggested table:** show revenue at 0, −3, −6 and −9 points.

That would make the case more persuasive, not less.

The recommendation's "at least £204,000" should go. The figure is neither a floor nor correctly calculated.

## 3. The two-night minimum conflicts with your largest Saturday segment

Section 4 says wedding guests at Quayside Hall make up about 38% of Saturday bookings, and that they typically arrive Saturday and leave Sunday. That is exactly the stay pattern a two-night minimum blocks. The proposal doesn't address this conflict.

- **Already-contracted wedding blocks** are presumably protected as "group rates already contracted."
- **New wedding blocks and individual wedding guests booking direct** would be turned away or forced to pay for a night they don't want. Many would book elsewhere, and the relationship with Quayside Hall (and couples' willingness to recommend you) could suffer.

**Unconstrained Saturdays.** You sold out 31 Saturdays, so about 21 were not sold out. On those nights the minimum turns away single-night business you had room for. A minimum stay helps only when demand clearly exceeds supply.

**Unquantified gain.** The extra Friday/Sunday revenue is described as "material" but not estimated. It could be net negative once lost Saturday-only guests are counted. Leaving it out is therefore not conservative either.

**Suggested fix:** apply the minimum selectively, only on high-demand Saturdays (for example when pick-up is above a threshold X weeks out). Exempt wedding blocks and agree an approach with Quayside Hall. Model the expected displacement.

## 4. Monitoring

- **Peak-season launch.** Starting on 1 June means the first test is the peak summer months, when strong demand will hide price sensitivity. The trigger may not fire until autumn, when the risk is higher.
- **Two changes at once.** Introducing the rate rise and the minimum stay together means you can't tell which one caused any occupancy change. Consider staggering them, or at least tracking Saturday-only demand separately.
- **Weak response.** "Review the rate" is soft. State what will happen if the trigger fires (for example revert to £155, or lift the minimum).
- **Better leading indicators.** Measure the trigger against the comp set (for example STR market share or rate index), not only against 2025, and look at forward pick-up rather than actualised monthly occupancy. That is how you would genuinely "see it within a month."

## 5. Smaller points

- Two weeks' notice to OTAs may be tight under some channel contracts; worth checking.
- The comp-set range (£165–180) should be dated and broken down by season. Competitors' summer rates may not reflect their shoulder-month rates.
- A two-night stay including Saturday may mean Saturday plus Sunday at a midweek rate. Clarify which rate applies to the Sunday night.

## Suggested revisions in priority order

1. Fix the room count and recalculate on BAR-only, net-of-commission volume.
2. Replace the June→July claim with a year-on-year or pick-up comparison, or present it only as weak supporting evidence.
3. Show an occupancy sensitivity table with the break-even point.
4. Rework the two-night minimum around the wedding segment and apply it only on high-demand dates.
5. Firm up the monitoring trigger and decide whether to stagger the two changes.

**One more thing:** the proposal is dated April 2026 for a 1 June start, and it's now November. If the change went ahead, you have five months of actual 2026 results (including a full low-demand comparison in October). That data would be far stronger evidence than anything in this draft, and it's worth using before this goes any further.
